In the weeks leading up to the New York City mayoral election, Chris Van
Hollen was angry.

Zohran Mamdani, a 33-year-old democratic socialist, just upended U.S.
politics, winning the Democratic primary and becoming the nominee to lead the
biggest city in the country.

While Mamdani was impressing voters, many Democratic officials refused to
endorse him, or continued to implicitly or explicitly undermine him. Van
Hollen, who endorsed Mamdani in September, slammed them for remaining mum.

**" Many Democratic members of the Senate and the House delegations
representing New York have stayed on the sidelines,"** he
[said](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/09/13/us/politics/van-hollen-zohran-
mamdani.html). **" That kind of spineless politics is what people are sick
of."**

The race, of course, was between Mamdani; Curtis Sliwa, the Republican; and
Andrew Cuomo, an alleged sexual abuser funded by Trump-allied billionaires who
lost the primary and decided to run as an independent.

One of the New York pols keeping silent was Chuck Schumer, Democrats' pro-
Israel Senate minority leader, who refused to say whom he was supporting in
the race - and never ended up endorsing.

A year later, Democrats have secured a significant Senate majority, fueled in
part by candidates across the country adopting the same messaging focus on
"affordability" as Mamdani.

Who will that majority choose to lead them now? The senator who rallied behind
a mayor who's changed the American political landscape, who has led by
example, traveling to El Salvador and Palestine to confront abuses by Trump
and Israel? Or the party's current Senate leader, who has again and again
bailed out Republicans, sacrificed Democrats' upper hand, done little to slow
Trump's immigration terror machine, and unconditionally supported Israel's
genocidal U.S. tax-funded violence?

No challenger to Schumer has emerged yet, even as his approval ratings
[continue to fall](https://www.realclearpolling.com/polls/favorability/chuck-
schumer). Still, a number of Democrats have expressed interest in new
